sec1.titulo: Half of their questions are about people
abertura: A buyer asks about numbers and about people, in roughly equal measure. The people questions are the ones you answer without preparing.
Mark the three statements that are true.

itens.t: Describing who decides what is as much of the conversation as the figures.
A missing verb ending changes the meaning of the sentence.
The form slips most when the sentence gets long.
Knowing the rule is enough to say it right under pressure.
Correcting yourself mid-sentence is better than stopping to fix it.
If you speak slowly enough, the ending takes care of itself.

sec1.rationale: The ending does not carry meaning -- nobody misunderstands *he want*. It carries something else: whether the person listening spends any attention on your English instead of on your answer.

nota.titulo: Why this lesson, and why now
nota.texto: You named this one yourself: she like, he have. You know the rule — so this lesson explains almost nothing and drills a lot. The target is not knowing it. It is having it survive a long sentence about something else.

doc.texto:
Your side
• Head of Delivery — runs the delivery teams and decides who goes on which account.
• CFO — owns the numbers the buyer asked for, and signs off what leaves the company.
• Head of People — knows who on the team already works in English, and who does not.
• You — decide whether this conversation happens at all.

Their side
• Mark — runs finance, and wants the recurring revenue number confirmed.
• Peter — advises them, and keeps coming back to delivery.
• Diane — leads corporate development, and writes the emails.
• Their board — meets monthly, and approves the structure.

abertura: Who would answer each of these questions?

itens.t: "How much of the revenue is recurring?"
"Who would be on our account in the first year?"
"How many of the team already work in English?"
"Would you consider a minority position?"
"Can we see the last three years audited?"
"Are you selling because you want out?"

nota.titulo: Two of the six are only yours
nota.texto: Everything factual can be delegated. The two that cannot are the two about intention — and those are the ones that get asked in English, live, with no preparation.

abertura: Mark the sentences that are correct. Two of the six are not.

itens.t: Our Head of Delivery decides who goes on each account.
Their CFO want the recurring number confirmed.
The team handles three markets from São José.
She report to me, and I report to the board.
Their board meets once a month.
Peter keeps coming back to delivery.

sec3.rationale: Both of the wrong ones are third person singular with the ending missing. Nothing about them is hard to understand -- and that is exactly why they survive for years.

nota.texto: Do not look for the rule. Look at what is different between the four that are right and the two that are not, and say it out loud before you check — in class, that is the whole of stage 3.

abertura: One of the two endings is the one that belongs there.

itens.t: Our CFO
The delivery teams
Their adviser
I
alts: decide whether we talk at all
decides whether we talk at all
itens.ok: decide whether we talk at all

itens.t: Their board
My partners and I

nota.titulo: The whole form, in one line
nota.texto: He, she and it take the -s. I, you, we and they do not. American English treats the team and the board as one thing, so they take it too.

abertura: The information does not change. Only the subject does -- and with it, the verb.

itens.t: I run the delivery side. → She ...
They handle three markets. → He ...
She has the audited accounts. → We ...
He does the pricing. → They ...
We decide the structure. → The board ...
You know who speaks English. → My Head of People ...

nota.texto: Not here. It slips three clauses into a sentence about something else, when the subject changed two clauses ago and you are thinking about the answer. That is what the ninety seconds in class are for.

sec6.titulo: Four of your eight, written down first
abertura: Complete the sentences with the verb in brackets. This is half of what you will say in class.
Use the real names and real roles from your own company if you prefer.
itens: Our Head of Delivery {decides|120px} (decide) who goes on each account.
Their CFO {wants|110px} (want) the recurring number confirmed before the call.
My Head of People {knows|110px} (know) exactly who already works in English.
Their board {meets|100px} (meet) once a month and {approves|120px} (approve) the structure.
My partners and I {hold|100px} (hold) the majority, and I {decide|110px} (decide) whether this conversation happens.

nota.titulo: No word bank here, on purpose
nota.texto: The word is already given to you in brackets. What is being asked for is the form of it — which is the whole point, and which a list of options would hand you for free.

callout.texto: Two numbers: how often the form came out right in the drill, and how often it came out right when you were describing eight people under a clock. The distance between those two numbers is what ‘knowing the rule’ is worth in a real conversation.

abertura: Record a short voice message, if you would like to.

callout.texto:
Describe your actual leadership team — four people, one sentence each.

What you are trying to do: say what each one decides, not what each one is called. Sixty seconds.

abertura: Write the other four sentences -- the ones you did not write in the pre-class.

callout.texto: Four sentences you can watch. Eight is where the attention moves to the content and the form has to hold on its own — which is the only condition that matters in a real conversation.
